sections.normalized_html:
Which of the following statements must be true regarding any tetrahedron?

  1. It has [MATH: 6] faces

  2. It has [MATH: 6] edges

  3. It has [MATH: 4] vertices
sections.readable_text:
Which of the following statements must be true regarding any tetrahedron?

1. It has [MATH: 6] faces
2. It has [MATH: 6] edges
3. It has [MATH: 4] vertices

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Below is an example of a tetrahedron.

Let's examine our statements in turn.

  • Statement I is false. A tetrahedron is a regular polyhedron that

    • consists of [MATH: 4] congruent faces, each in the form of an equilateral triangle, and

    • exactly [MATH: 3] faces meet at each vertex.

  • Statement II is true. Since there are [MATH: F=4] faces, each in the form of a triangle, we have [MATH: S = 4 \cdot 3 = 12] sides combined. Now, each edge of the polyhedron is created when two face sides coincide. So, the number of edges of the tetrahedron must be equal to [MATH: \dfrac{S}{2} = \dfrac{12}{2} = 6.]

  • Statement III is true. Substituting the number of edges [MATH: E=6] and the number of faces [MATH: F=4] into Euler's formula, we can solve for the number of vertices [MATH: V] as follows: [MATH: V − E + F|= 2; V − (6) + (4)|= 2; V − 2|= 2; V|= 4]

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

items.title: Classifying Platonic Solids According to Their Faces

sections.normalized_html: We can classify Platonic solids according to their faces.
sections.readable_text: We can classify Platonic solids according to their faces.

sections.normalized_html:
• There are three Platonic solids with triangular faces:

    • the tetrahedron, where exactly [MATH: 3] equilateral triangles meet at each vertex

    • the octahedron, where exactly [MATH: 4] equilateral triangles meet at each vertex

    • the icosahedron, where exactly [MATH: 5] equilateral triangles meet at each vertex

    Note that a convex polyhedron cannot have more than [MATH: 5] equilateral triangles meeting at each vertex. The interior angles of an equilateral triangle have a measure of [MATH: 60^\circ.] So, if we take [MATH: 6] or more triangles, the sum of the face angles (the [MATH: 2]D interior angles of the triangles that meet at a vertex) will be [MATH: 360^\circ] or more. If the sum is exactly [MATH: 360^\circ], the faces lie flat in a plane. If it is greater than [MATH: 360^\circ], the faces would overlap, so no [MATH: 3]D convex solid can be formed.

Item 13 — Example: Identifying Properties of Platonic Solids

Example Prompt:
Which of the following statements must be true regarding any tetrahedron?

1. It has [MATH: 6] faces
2. It has [MATH: 6] edges
3. It has [MATH: 4] vertices

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Below is an example of a tetrahedron.

[IMG: /graphics/364f12d988cd5cc19fb3a6e1186ef174]

Let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. A tetrahedron is a regular polyhedron that

- consists of [MATH: 4] congruent faces, each in the form of an equilateral triangle, and
- exactly [MATH: 3] faces meet at each vertex.
- Statement II is true. Since there are [MATH: F=4] faces, each in the form of a triangle, we have
[MATH: S = 4 \cdot 3 = 12]
sides combined. Now, each edge of the polyhedron is created when two face sides coincide. So, the number of edges of the tetrahedron must be equal to
[MATH: \dfrac{S}{2} = \dfrac{12}{2} = 6.]
- Statement III is true. Substituting the number of edges [MATH: E=6] and the number of faces [MATH: F=4] into Euler's formula, we can solve for the number of vertices [MATH: V] as follows:
[MATH: V − E + F|= 2; V − (6) + (4)|= 2; V − 2|= 2; V|= 4]

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

Item 17 — Tutorial: Classifying Platonic Solids According to Their Faces

Content:
We can classify Platonic solids according to their faces.

Content:
- There are three Platonic solids with triangular faces:

- the tetrahedron, where exactly [MATH: 3] equilateral triangles meet at each vertex
- the octahedron, where exactly [MATH: 4] equilateral triangles meet at each vertex
- the icosahedron, where exactly [MATH: 5] equilateral triangles meet at each vertex

[IMG: /graphics/3be47c9e956d19e48a59764e60a3c4b6]

Note that a convex polyhedron cannot have more than [MATH: 5] equilateral triangles meeting at each vertex. The interior angles of an equilateral triangle have a measure of [MATH: 60^\circ.] So, if we take [MATH: 6] or more triangles, the sum of the face angles (the [MATH: 2]D interior angles of the triangles that meet at a vertex) will be [MATH: 360^\circ] or more. If the sum is exactly [MATH: 360^\circ], the faces lie flat in a plane. If it is greater than [MATH: 360^\circ], the faces would overlap, so no [MATH: 3]D convex solid can be formed.

Content:
- The cube is the only Platonic solid with rectangular faces. In this case, exactly [MATH: 3] squares meet at each vertex.

[IMG: /graphics/09b6539c4683cf1089609a4c862b771d]

Note that a convex polyhedron cannot have more than [MATH: 3] squares meeting at each vertex. The interior angles of a square have a measure of [MATH: 90^\circ.] So, if we take [MATH: 4] or more squares, the sum of the face angles (the [MATH: 2]D interior angles of the triangles that meet at a vertex) will be [MATH: 360^\circ] or more. If the sum is exactly [MATH: 360^\circ], the faces lie flat in a plane. If it is greater than [MATH: 360^\circ], the faces would overlap, so no [MATH: 3]D convex solid can be formed.

Content:
- The dodecahedron is the only Platonic solid with pentagonal faces. In this case, exactly [MATH: 3] regular pentagons meet at each vertex.

[IMG: /graphics/b133aa906f622a1094663545c1d65c62]

Note that a convex polyhedron cannot have more than [MATH: 3] regular pentagons meeting at each vertex. The internal angles of a regular pentagon have a measure of [MATH: 108^\circ.] So, if we take [MATH: 4] or more pentagons, the combined measure of all the interior angles that meet at a vertex will be more than [MATH: 360^\circ.]
